candidates.text:
Just so everybody gets a clear image about this.
​If the board removes him as CEO, several clear boundaries apply:

• Every share Jensen Huang already owns outright is his legal property. He retains full voting rights for those shares and can hold them, borrow against them, or dump them on the open market whenever he chooses (subject only to standard SEC insider trading blackout windows if he remains on the board, or Rule 144 volume limits if he steps down completely).

• The only shares a board can claw back or cancel upon termination are unvested performance stock units (PSUs) or restricted stock units (RSUs) that have not yet met their time or performance milestones. Given that Jensen co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and holds roughly 3.5% of the company outright, the vast majority of his multi-billion-dollar stake is long since vested. 

• Because he is Nvidia's largest individual shareholder, firing him against his will creates an immediate existential headache for the board. As an outside shareholder, he could launch a proxy fight to replace the board directors at the next annual meeting, start a rival silicon venture and poach Nvidia's top CUDA and architecture leads, or threaten to liquidate tens of billions of dollars in stock, cratering the share price for institutional investors.

In short, firing a founder who owns over $100 billion in vested stock does not strip him of power; it just turns him into an activist shareholder with infinite capital and zero fiduciary obligations to protect the board.

Founder succession is an open problem. 

Successful founders are themselves odd ducks who surround themselves with people who complement their strengths and weaknesses.

By definition, the people who surround a founder are very different from the founder.

But when a founder leaves, we promote the most successful subordinate into an organizational spot which they, almost by definition, don’t fit. 

Replacing a visionary founder CEO with a CFO or COO is comically stupid. Yet it is considered the best practice.

I don’t know the answer to this problem,  and although I have some ideas, I am nowhere close to ready to test them on my own business :)

A common slippery rope with many men who think that they can outsource everything with money, is that at some point, they also stop thinking by themselves (they can always hire "experts"), they are no longer capable of any compromise and isolate themselves in a bubble of "yes people" ("this conflict isn't worth my time, I have plenty of other options"), and they even forget what it's like to build a meaningful bond with someone else, including with their own wife, children, parents ("I can hire people for the household chores, I'm being a great husband, babysitters can take care of the kids and then expensive private schools will give them the best education, I'm being a great father, I'm sending my parents to a retirement home, I'm being a great son.")

The biggest irony of a lot of smart people is how, in their quest of hyper-efficiency and maximization of every output, they become completely disconnected with their own emotions (but call it "detachment") and they often end up being susceptible to the most timelessly common blunders that keep leading many men to their ruin generation after generation.

The important thing we should all keep in mind: the smarter you are, the more sophisticated and believable your self-talk, and the easier it actually becomes to lie to yourself.

Nvidia’s board placed the CFO as interim CEO of the company. 

That’s a really stupid decision. 

The CEO is a General Manager. 

The right interim leader would be Ian Buck who runs the largest and fastest growing Datacenter business. 

Satya Nadella previously ran Azure - the largest and fastest growing business. 

Andy Jassy led AWS - Amazon’s largest and fastest growing business. 

General Managers lead, make trade-offs, hire, ship…

The life of a CFO is living in a spreadsheet - not the messiness of the real world. 

The only good reason not to put Ian in as Interim CEO is if the board thought he might be knowingly caught up in export violations swirling the firm. 

The General Manager would of course know all these details. 

So, either the board is stupid or they have legitimate deeper concerns. 

Either way, appointing the CFO as CEO raises questions, not confidence.
